situationBrief.title: The Class 10 Concord Casebook
situationBrief.description: Senior editors Mira, Arjun, and ShukaJi are auditing complex school notices packed with 'the number of vs a number of', collective nouns, fractions, and relative pronoun antecedents.

storyIntro.previewSectionTitle: High-level traps pinned to the board
scatteredFragments: One of the boys who has/have ...

beats.speaker: mira
beats.dialogue: Look at these two sentences side by side: 'The number of volunteers is rising' and 'A number of volunteers are helping.' Both mention volunteers—why do their verbs flip?

beats.speaker: arjun
beats.actionLabel: Examines collective nouns and relative clauses
beats.dialogue: And look at this clause case: 'She is one of the students who has/have won scholarships.' Does 'who' refer back to 'one' or to 'students'?
beats.cardPreviewText: The number of volunteers is rising.

beats.speaker: shuka
beats.dialogue: In Class 10, every verb still locks onto its true head—whether that is 'number' vs 'a number of', an undivided vs divided collective, a fraction's 'of'-noun, or a relative pronoun's antecedent. Let us crack every case!

grammarOutcomes: Distinguish 'the number of + plural noun' (singular verb) from 'a number of + plural noun' (plural verb), and apply fraction/percentage concord.
Choose singular vs plural verbs for collective nouns (acting as one unit vs divided individuals), 'the + adjective' ('the brave are'), and plural-form titles/countries.
Trace relative pronoun antecedents ('one of the girls who are...') accurately and apply formal concord with 'neither of / none of' alongside Odisha's informal note.
learningObjectives.knowledgeOutcome: Edit Class 10 school publications, ISRO/science reports, and literary book notices with total agreement accuracy.

sourceReferences.bookTitle: Learn and Practise Grammar Class - X
sourceReferences.chapter: Chapter 3: Subject – Verb Agreement (Rules 1a–16) & Ch. 4 p. 31
sourceReferences.note: Teaches 16 formal SVA rules including preparatory there/it, unit sums, 'and' single notion vs compound, collective nouns unit vs individuals, police/cattle, uncountables, intervening modifiers, either/neither/none of (+ informal note), one vs two determiners, fractions/percentages, 'the number of' vs 'a number of', '-s' nouns, 'with/as well as', 'not only...but also', 'the + adjective', plural titles, and relative pronoun antecedents.

sourceReferences.bookTitle: A NEW METHOD English Grammar For Class IX & X
sourceReferences.note: Combined Classes IX & X rules: 'The Secretary and Headmaster is' vs 'The Secretary and the Headmaster are', 'Many a man has', 'neither of' singular, and '-s' nouns.

sourceReferences.bookTitle: A Practice Book of ENGLISH GRAMMAR & COMPOSITION (GRAMMAR IN USE) for Class IX
sourceReferences.note: Cross-board reference for collective nouns, plural titles, and relative pronouns (Note: no Class 10 PSEB textbook was supplied among sources).
Synthesises Odisha X Ch. 3 with Assam IX-X and notes explicitly that no Class 10 PSEB textbook was provided.

sentences.title: Case 1: 'The Number of' vs 'A Number of'
sentences.rawText: The number of science projects in our fair is growing.
sentences.note: 'The number of + plural noun' means ONE count/figure → singular verb ('is'); 'A number of + plural noun' means 'several/many' → plural verb ('are').

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: 'The number' is singular; compare with 'A number' (= many).
Not the head of 'The number of...'.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: 'The number of + plural noun' refers to ONE single count/figure, so it takes a singular verb ('is').

groups.label: Subject
groups.questionPrompt: What is growing—the single count or individual projects?
groups.plainExplanation: 'The number' (a single count) is the Subject head.
groups.textbookRule: Odisha Class X Rule 9c (p. 27): 'A number of + plural noun' takes a plural verb (= many), while 'The number of + plural noun' takes a singular verb.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.textbookRule: Say 'The number of projects IS growing' vs 'A number of projects ARE ready'.

structureSummary.subjectText: The number of science projects in our fair

sentences.title: Case 2: Collective Nouns (Unit vs Individuals)
sentences.rawText: The jury are divided in their opinions.
sentences.note: A collective noun ('jury', 'committee', 'team') takes a singular verb when acting as ONE unit, and a plural verb when members act individually.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Refers to individual judges disagreeing here.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Clues 'divided' and 'their opinions' show separate members → plural verb 'are'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Agrees with individual members of the jury.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Plural verb used because members hold different opinions.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: Clues 'divided' and 'their opinions' show the members acting as separate individuals, not one united voice.

groups.label: Subject
groups.questionPrompt: Are the members acting as one voice or separately?
groups.plainExplanation: 'The jury' is divided into separate individuals here.
groups.textbookRule: Odisha Class X Rule 4a (p. 25) & PSEB IX Rule 10 (p. 99): Collective nouns take singular when acting as one body ('The committee IS unanimous') and plural when acting individually ('The jury ARE divided in their opinions').

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'are divided in their opinions' uses plural 'are'.
groups.textbookRule: Look for clues like 'its decision' (singular) vs 'their opinions' (plural).

structureSummary.patternNote: Collective acting as one unit → singular; divided individuals → plural.

sentences.title: Case 3: Relative Pronoun Antecedent
sentences.rawText: Riya is one of the students who have won medals.
sentences.note: Inside '...one of the [plural noun] who...', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'the students' (plural), so the verb after 'who' is 'have'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: One member of the medal-winning group.
The whole group who won medals.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Relative pronoun 'who' directly refers back to plural 'students'!
Copies plural number from its antecedent 'students'.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: Ask 'Who has/have won medals?'—the whole group of 'students' (plural), not just 'one'!

groups.label: Subject
groups.textbookRule: Odisha Class X Rule 16 (p. 29) & PSEB IX Rule 12 (p. 99): The verb after a relative pronoun ('who/which/that') agrees with its antecedent ('students' → 'have').

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'who' refers to 'students' (plural), so 'have won' is plural.
groups.textbookRule: Compare: 'She is the ONLY one of the students who HAS...' vs 'She is one of the students who HAVE...'.

relationships.label: have ← who ← students
relationships.explanation: Relative pronoun 'who' inherits plural number from 'students'.

structureSummary.predicateText: is one of the students who have won medals
structureSummary.patternNote: Relative clause verb matches its antecedent ('students' → 'have').

sentences.title: Case 4: Fractions, Percentages & 'The + Adjective'
sentences.rawText: Two-thirds of the library books are already catalogued.
sentences.note: With fractions or percentages ('two-thirds of', 'half of', '40% of'), look at the noun AFTER 'of' to pick the verb!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Unlike regular 'of'-phrases, fractions/percentages take their number from the noun after 'of'!

tokens.meaningInSentence: Plural countable noun after 'of' → plural verb!
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Because 'books' is plural, 'Two-thirds of the books' takes plural 'are'.
Compare 'Two-thirds of the water IS clean' (uncountable → singular).

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: For fractions and percentages ('two-thirds of', 'a lot of'), plural countable nouns after 'of' ('books') take plural 'are', while uncountable nouns ('water') take singular 'is'.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'books' is plural countable, so the fraction is plural.
groups.textbookRule: Odisha Class X Rule 8 & 9a (pp. 26-27): Fractions, percentages, 'a lot of', and 'some of' match the noun after 'of'.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.textbookRule: Uncountable after 'of' → singular ('Two-thirds of the land IS fertile').

relationships.label: are ← books (after fraction)
relationships.explanation: Fractions match the number of the noun following 'of'.

structureSummary.patternNote: Fraction/percentage/'a lot of' → check noun after 'of' ('books' = plural, 'water' = singular).

teachingSequence.title: 'The Number of' vs 'A Number of'
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: 'The number of...' = ONE single figure (singular); 'A number of...' = MANY (plural).
teachingSequence.explanation: Odisha Class X Rule 9c sets a classic exam trap: 'The number of science projects is growing' (focuses on ONE rising figure → 'is'), whereas 'A number of science projects are ready' means 'several projects' → 'are'. One small article ('The' vs 'A') flips the verb!

agreementData.interveningText: of science projects in our fair
agreementData.ruleSummary: 'The number of + plural noun' → singular verb; 'A number of + plural noun' → plural verb.
agreementData.contrastIncorrectText: The number of science projects in our fair are growing.
agreementData.contrastReason: It is the single count ('The number') that is growing, not each separate project.

teachingSequence.title: Collective Nouns: One Unit vs Individuals
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Does the group act together ('its') or disagree individually ('their')?
teachingSequence.explanation: In Odisha Class X Rule 4a, collective nouns ('jury, committee, team, government') take a SINGULAR verb when acting as one body ('The committee has made its decision'), and a PLURAL verb when members act separately ('The jury are divided in their opinions').

agreementData.ruleSummary: Watch for agreement clues in the sentence: 'its / unanimous' → singular; 'their / divided' → plural. Also remember 'police / people / cattle / poultry' ALWAYS take plural verbs!

teachingSequence.title: Fractions, Percentages & 'A Lot of'
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: With fractions and percentages, look AFTER 'of' to decide the verb!
teachingSequence.explanation: Here is an essential exception to the 'ignore of-phrases' rule! When the Subject starts with a fraction, percentage, 'half of', 'a lot of', or 'some of', look at the noun AFTER 'of': plural countable ('books') → 'are'; uncountable ('water', 'rice', 'scenery') → 'is'.

agreementData.ruleSummary: Compare: 'Two-thirds of the books ARE catalogued' vs 'Two-thirds of the rainwater IS stored cleanly'.

teachingSequence.title: Relative Pronoun Antecedents
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: In 'one of the students who...', trace 'who' back to 'students', NOT 'one'!
teachingSequence.explanation: Odisha Class X Rule 16 solves one of the trickiest Class 10 questions! In 'Riya is one of the students who have won medals', several students won medals and Riya is one of them. So 'who' points to plural 'students', locking onto 'have'.

agreementData.ruleSummary: A verb after 'who / which / that' agrees with the antecedent right before the pronoun—unless 'the ONLY one of...' appears.
agreementData.contrastIncorrectText: Riya is one of the students who has won medals.
agreementData.contrastReason: More than one student won medals; 'who' stands for 'the students'.

teachingSequence.title: 'The + Adjective' & Plural-Form Titles
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: 'The brave ARE respected' (plural class), while 'Gulliver's Travels IS famous' (one book)!
teachingSequence.explanation: Odisha Class X Rules 14 & 15 contrast two tricky patterns: (1) 'The + adjective' referring to a whole group of people ('the rich', 'the brave', 'the blind') always takes a PLURAL verb ('The brave are honoured'). (2) Plural-looking book titles and country names ('Gulliver's Travels', 'The United States') refer to ONE work or nation → SINGULAR verb ('is').

agreementData.ruleSummary: Also note Assam & Odisha Class X's rule on 'with / as well as' (first subject wins) vs 'not only...but also / neither...nor' (nearer subject wins), and 'Many a student HAS tried'.

teachingSequence.title: Neither of / None of & One vs Two Determiners
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Formal singular for 'neither of', and check whether 'the' is repeated!
teachingSequence.explanation: Two final senior checks: (1) 'The Secretary and Headmaster IS coming' (1 'the' = 1 person) vs 'The Secretary and the Headmaster ARE coming' (2 'the's = 2 people). (2) In formal exams, 'neither of / none of / either of + plural noun' takes a SINGULAR verb ('Neither of the reports is late').

agreementData.subjectHeadText: Neither of / None of + plural noun
agreementData.ruleSummary: Use formal singular for 'neither of / none of / each of / one of' in exams.
agreementData.informalUsageNote: Odisha Class X Rule 7a (p. 26) explicitly notes that plural verbs occur after 'neither of / none of' in informal speech, whereas PSEB and Assam mandate singular strictly. Note: no Class 10 PSEB book was supplied in the source files.

teachingSequence.title: Senior Detective Verification Checklist
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: 1. Cross out modifiers. 2. Check rule family. 3. Lock the finite verb.
teachingSequence.explanation: Before answering any Class 10 SVA question: (1) Identify whether the Subject is a normal head-noun ('The number of'), a fraction/portion ('Two-thirds of'), a collective ('jury'), or a relative antecedent ('students who...'). (2) Match Number and Person precisely!

agreementData.ruleSummary: Odisha X Ch. 4 p. 31 reminds us: only finite verbs show tense and Subject–Verb Agreement; non-finites ('to read', 'reading') never change for Subject number.

teachingSequence.title: Inspect Words Before Senior Detective Lab
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Tap 'Two-thirds', 'books', or 'are' above to inspect how they lock, then enter Guided Practice.
teachingSequence.explanation: Tap any token above to verify its role, then open Guided Practice to solve all 6 Class 10 detective cases!

wordLabActivities.title: A. Spot the Antecedent Controlling 'who'
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap the ONE noun that 'who' refers back to and that controls 'play'.

sentence.title: Senior Clue A
sentence.rawText: Arjun is one of the athletes who play kho-kho.

structureSummary.predicateText: is one of the athletes who play kho-kho

wordLabActivities.correctFeedback: Exact! 'who' stands for 'athletes' (plural), which is why the verb is plural 'play'.
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Tap ONLY the plural noun standing right before 'who' ('athletes').
wordLabActivities.hint: Ask: Does ONLY one athlete play kho-kho, or do ALL the 'athletes' play kho-kho?

wordLabActivities.title: B. Sort Class 10 Subjects Into Singular vs Plural
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap each Subject card and sort whether it takes a Singular Verb or Plural Verb.
wordLabActivities.promptText: 1. Tap a Subject card below, then tap Singular Verb or Plural Verb:

items.explanation: 'The number of...' refers to one count.
'The + adjective' denoting people is always plural.
One book title takes a singular verb.
'Many a + singular noun' takes a singular verb.

wordLabActivities.completeFeedback: Clean 6/6! You navigated Class 10's trickiest agreement patterns accurately.
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Remember: 'The number of' & 'Many a' = singular; 'A number of', 'The brave', & fractions + plural nouns = plural.

wordLabActivities.title: C. Assemble a 'Not Only ... But Also' Sentence
wordLabActivities.instruction: Arrange the tiles so the verb agrees with the NEARER subject ('the students').
wordLabActivities.promptContext: With 'not only...but also', the nearer subject controls the verb.
wordLabActivities.subjectText: Not only the teacher but also the students
wordLabActivities.correctFeedback: Exact! Plural 'the students' is closer to the verb, locking onto 'were'.
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Order: 'Not only the teacher' + 'but also' + 'the students' + 'were' + 'excited about ISRO.'

wordLabActivities.title: D. Flip the Noun After 'of', Flip the Verb!
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap both options after 'Half of the' to see how countable vs uncountable nouns control the verb.
wordLabActivities.slotLabel: Uncountable vs Plural Countable After Fraction:

options.meaningEffect: 'curd' is uncountable (like milk, rice, scenery) → singular 'is'.

wordLabActivities.takeaway: For fractions and percentages, uncountable nouns after 'of' take singular verbs, while plural countables take plural verbs!

wordLabActivities.title: E. Choose the Collective Noun Verb
wordLabActivities.instruction: Read the clue ('its unanimous report') and select the accurate verb.

options.feedback: 'its unanimous report' shows the committee acted as ONE united body, so use singular 'has'.
Spot on! Acting as one united body ('its unanimous report') calls for singular 'has'.
'are' is plural and doesn't pair with 'submitted' to form Present Perfect active.

wordLabActivities.title: F. Repair the Uncountable Furniture Trap
wordLabActivities.instruction: Inspect this flawed school inventory line and diagnose the error.
wordLabActivities.brokenSentence: All the new wooden furniture in the hall are durable.
wordLabActivities.repairedSentence: All the new wooden furniture in the hall is durable.
wordLabActivities.question: Why must 'are' become 'is'?

options.label: Nouns like 'furniture', 'scenery', 'luggage', and 'clothing' are uncountable and always take a singular verb ('is').
options.feedback: Exact! Odisha Class X Rule 5 classifies furniture, clothing, food, and scenery as singular uncountables.

options.label: 'All' always forces a plural verb regardless of the noun.
options.feedback: 'All' can be singular with uncountable nouns ('All the water is clean') or plural with countables ('All the books are new').

options.label: Because 'hall' is singular at the end of the phrase.
options.feedback: 'in the hall' is just a prepositional modifier; 'furniture' is the singular uncountable Subject head.

independentPractice.cueText: Check whether 'The' or 'A' precedes 'number of' before locking the verb.
independentPractice.title: Challenge 1: The Number vs A Number Paradox
independentPractice.instruction: Tap the two key words at the start that decide whether the verb is singular or plural, then choose the verb.
independentPractice.targetPrompt: Step 1: Tap the first two words ('The' or 'A' + 'number')

sentence.title: Independent Check 1
sentence.rawText: A number of young astronomers [?] observing the eclipse tonight.

independentPractice.imperativeQuestion: Step 2: Which auxiliary fits 'A number of young astronomers _____ observing...'?

imperativeOptions.label: is
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'The number of' takes 'is', whereas 'A number of' means 'many' and takes plural 'are'!

imperativeOptions.label: are
imperativeOptions.feedback: Spot on! 'A number of + plural noun' means several/many, taking plural 'are'.

imperativeOptions.label: was
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'was' is singular and past, clashing with 'tonight' and 'A number of'.

independentPractice.retrySubjectFeedback: Tap ONLY the first two words: 'A' and 'number'.

independentPractice.cueText: Remember: 'The + adjective' denoting a class of people takes a plural verb.
independentPractice.title: Challenge 2: 'The + Adjective' & 'The United States'
independentPractice.instruction: Pick the accurate verb to complete the sentence.

sentence.title: Independent Check 2
sentence.rawText: In every society, the honest and hardworking _____ deeply respected.

independentPractice.imperativeQuestion: Which verb completes this sentence accurately?

imperativeOptions.label: is
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'the + adjective' here refers to all honest and hardworking people (plural), not one person.

imperativeOptions.label: are
imperativeOptions.feedback: Exact! Odisha Class X Rule 14 teaches that 'the + adjective' referring to a class of people ('the rich', 'the blind', 'the honest') takes a plural verb ('are').

independentPractice.title: Challenge 3: Senior Detective Final Audit
independentPractice.instruction: Identify the ONE sentence that follows every Class 10 Subject–Verb Agreement rule.

structureSummary.subjectText: Forty percent of the fresh water

imperativeOptions.label: Forty percent of the fresh water are saved through rainwater harvesting.
imperativeOptions.feedback: After a percentage, look at 'water' (uncountable) → singular 'is'.

imperativeOptions.label: Subhas Chandra Bose is one of the leaders who inspire young Indians.
imperativeOptions.feedback: Accurate! Antecedent of 'who' is plural 'leaders', taking plural 'inspire'.

imperativeOptions.label: Gulliver's Travels are an unforgettable adventure story.
imperativeOptions.feedback: One book title ('Gulliver's Travels') takes a singular verb ('is').

independentPractice.successFeedback: Senior casebook closed! Outstanding mastery of Class 10 Subject–Verb Agreement.

completionSummary.headline: Senior Casebook Solved! Mission 3 Complete!
completionSummary.celebrationMessage: You helped Mira, Arjun, and ShukaJi crack Class 10's toughest Subject–Verb Agreement cases!
learnedPoints: 'The number of + plural noun' takes a singular verb (one count), whereas 'A number of + plural noun' takes a plural verb (= many).
Fractions and percentages agree with the noun after 'of'; collective nouns take singular when united and plural when divided.

Relative clause verbs agree with their antecedent ('the students who HAVE...'); 'the + adjective' takes plural; plural titles/countries take singular; formal exams expect singular after 'neither of / none of'.
repairedMessages: The number of science projects in our fair is growing.
The jury are divided in their opinions.
Riya is one of the students who have won medals.
Two-thirds of the library books are already catalogued.
